name: AWS Glue
oneLiner: Serverless Spark ETL plus a data catalog; crawlers infer schema for you.
whatItIs: Glue is AWS's serverless data-integration service. Its two big pieces are the ETL engine — managed Apache Spark (and a Python-shell option) that you write jobs for, with no clusters to run — and the Glue Data Catalog, a central metadata store of your tables and schemas that Athena, Redshift Spectrum and EMR all share. Crawlers can scan S3 and infer table schemas automatically. Glue is the usual way to clean and reshape raw lake data into curated, query-ready Parquet on AWS.

inPractice.narrative: Raw JSON/CSV lands in an S3 bronze bucket. A Glue crawler infers its schema and registers a table in the Data Catalog. A Glue Spark job then cleans, joins and rewrites the data as partitioned Parquet in a curated bucket, updating the catalog. Athena and Redshift Spectrum immediately query those tables — because they read the same catalog Glue writes to. Glue is the transformation step that turns a raw lake into an analysis-ready one.

coreConcepts.detail: A shared metastore of databases, tables and schemas (Hive-compatible). It's the single source of truth Athena, Spectrum, EMR and Lake Formation all reference.
Jobs that scan a data source (e.g. S3 prefix), infer schema and partitions, and populate/refresh Catalog tables — saving manual DDL.
Serverless Spark jobs written in PySpark/Scala. You pick DPUs (workers); Glue spins them up, runs the job and tears them down — you never manage a cluster.
Glue's Spark-DataFrame-like abstraction that tolerates messy, evolving schemas and offers built-in transforms; convertible to/from normal Spark DataFrames.
A visual job builder, plus Python-shell jobs for lightweight tasks and Ray for Python-native scale — beyond full Spark.
Job bookmarks track what's already been processed so incremental runs skip old data — key for not reprocessing the whole lake each night.

whenToUse: Serverless Spark ETL to clean and reshape S3 data into curated Parquet.
Maintaining a central schema catalog shared by Athena, Spectrum and EMR.
Auto-discovering schemas of files in S3 with crawlers.
Incremental batch pipelines where you don't want to manage clusters.
Lightweight Python transforms (Python-shell jobs) without full Spark.
whenNotToUse: Sub-second/real-time streaming transforms at scale — consider Managed Flink (though Glue has streaming ETL).
Long-lived, heavily-tuned Spark clusters with custom software — EMR gives more control.
Simple event-glue with no data-processing shape — a Lambda is cheaper and simpler.
Interactive, notebook-driven exploration as the primary mode — use EMR/Studio notebooks or Athena.

keyFacts.label: Engine
keyFacts.value: Serverless Apache Spark (plus Python-shell and Ray jobs).

keyFacts.label: Catalog
keyFacts.value: Glue Data Catalog — Hive-compatible metastore shared AWS-wide.

keyFacts.label: Billing
keyFacts.value: Per DPU-hour while jobs/crawlers run (per-second, 1-min min).

keyFacts.label: Discovery
keyFacts.value: Crawlers infer schema and partitions automatically.

keyFacts.label: Ops
keyFacts.value: No clusters to provision or manage.

pricingShape: You pay per DPU-hour (data processing unit) for the time jobs and crawlers actually run, billed per-second with a small minimum — idle costs nothing because there's no standing cluster. The Data Catalog has a modest per-object storage and per-request charge that's negligible for most. Cost is driven by job runtime and worker count, so efficient Spark (right DPU count, partition pruning, bookmarks to avoid reprocessing) is what keeps the bill down. Crawlers add small recurring cost if scheduled frequently over large data.
gotchas: Crawlers can misinfer types or explode partitions on messy data — review inferred schemas rather than trusting them blindly.
Forgetting job bookmarks means reprocessing the entire dataset every run, wasting DPU-hours.
Spark cold-start/overhead makes Glue slow and pricey for tiny jobs — use Python-shell jobs for small tasks.
The Catalog is shared state: a bad crawler run or schema change can break Athena/Spectrum queries downstream.
DynamicFrames are convenient but sometimes slower/quirkier than plain Spark DataFrames — convert when you need raw Spark performance.
